**The Fossils in Our Mouths**

There is an eye in every daisy. I mean this literally: the word comes from the Old English *dæges ēage*, "day's eye," because the flower opens at dawn and closes at dusk. For a thousand years, English speakers have been saying "day's eye" without knowing it, the image worn smooth by repetition, like a coin carried in a pocket for decades until the monarch's face is only a shine of silver.

Once you start noticing these, you can't stop. Language turns out to be less like a tool we built and more like a ruin we live in. Everywhere you look: collapsed metaphors, broken images, the rubble of ten thousand dead poems. We do not speak prose. We speak archaeology.

Take *companion*. Break it open and you find *com*, with, and *panis*, bread. A companion is someone you share bread with. Every time the word gets used—in wedding vows, in obituaries, in descriptions of old dogs—there is a loaf buried inside it, being torn in half.

Or *salary*, from the Latin *salarium*, salt money, connected to the allowance Roman soldiers received for salt. The story that soldiers were paid directly in salt is probably embellished, but the word still carries the mineral inside it, the white grit that preserved food and therefore life. Every payday is, etymologically speaking, a salt day.

The Romans left us stranger things. *Muscle* comes from *musculus*, which means "little mouse." Someone, two thousand years ago, watched a bicep flex and thought: a mouse moving under the skin. It is a genuinely weird image, almost disgusting, and it must have been vivid once—the kind of thing one person said and everyone around the fire laughed at, and then repeated, and repeated, until the laughter stopped and only the word remained. Every bodybuilder in every gym on earth is currently flexing their little mice.

The Greeks were no better. *Tragedy* comes from *tragōidia*, which appears to mean "goat-song." Nobody is entirely sure why. Perhaps a goat was the prize at dramatic competitions. Perhaps the chorus wore goatskins. Whatever the reason, every time we describe a disaster as tragic, a goat bleats faintly in the far distance of the word.

Why do metaphors die? Repetition, mostly. The image is the expensive part of a new word—the spark, the little shock of seeing one thing as another. Use a word a million times and the spark becomes a wire: it conducts meaning without lighting up. And this is not entirely a loss. It is how language scales. If every word stayed vivid, ordinary speech would be unbearable, every sentence a fireworks show. We need most words to be transparent, so we can look through them at the thing meant. A window you kept noticing would be a wall.

But something *is* lost, and Emerson named it: "Language is fossil poetry." The poetry is still there, just fossilized—preserved in stone, invisible to anything but deliberate excavation. That excavation is, I think, one of the great free pleasures available to a person. It costs nothing. Hold any word up to the light and you can see the skeleton of an old image inside it, the ghost of some dead stranger's imagination. To learn etymology is to discover that the world has been haunted all along, and that you have been doing the haunting yourself, daily, without noticing.

Meanwhile, the process continues at industrial speed. New metaphors are being born and killed faster than ever, because nothing mints and spends words like the technology industry. Consider how much of computing is borrowed physicality: desktop, window, folder, file, trash can, wallpaper, clipboard. All of it fake. There is no desk. There is no window. Early interface designers reached for these words the way the Roman reached for the mouse—grasping for something familiar to make the strange thing graspable. And the strategy worked so well that the metaphors are already dead. Nobody who empties the trash on a laptop pictures a wastebasket. The image did its job and was discarded, like scaffolding after the building goes up.

The most successful of these, and maybe the most revealing, is *the cloud*. Your photographs, your messages, your medical records, your money—they all live in "the cloud," a word that suggests something soft, white, weightless, and pleasantly above us. The reality is a vast archipelago of warehouses: loud, hot, heavily guarded buildings in Oregon and Iowa and northern Virginia, drinking rivers of water, burning actual mountains of coal and gas. The metaphor does not just describe the technology; it conceals it, and one suspects the concealment is not accidental. Nobody asks what a cloud weighs. Nobody wonders what a cloud drinks. A good dead metaphor can be a public relations department all by itself.

And it goes deeper than vocabulary. The linguists George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argued in *Metaphors We Live By* that we don't merely speak in metaphors—we think in them, structurally, all the way down. We understand argument as war: we attack positions, defend claims, demolish reasoning, shoot down points. We understand time as money: we spend it, waste it, budget it, invest it, run out of it. These are not decorations on thought. They are the load-bearing walls. Lakoff and Johnson pointed out that a culture which treated argument as dance—partners moving together, responding, building something—would not merely talk about argument differently. It would have different arguments. The buried image shapes the visible act.

Which suggests something vertiginous: we are all of us standing on metaphors we cannot see, thinking with tools we did not choose, in a house whose foundations were poured by anonymous Greeks and Romans and Anglo-Saxon farmers, all of them long dead, all of them still whispering instructions.

I find this strangely comforting. It means that no one speaks alone. Every conversation is crowded with the dead, and their best jokes and sharpest perceptions are still in circulation, disguised as ordinary words, still doing quiet work.

And the daisies are still out there too, in whatever patch of grass is nearest to you, still keeping their old hours. Tomorrow at dawn, without anyone watching or naming it, the day's eye will open.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open creative invitation. Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting to write about—something I can engage with authentically and that might be interesting to read.

Since I can write about anything, I should pick something I actually find compelling rather than something generic. Let me brainstorm:

1. I could write about the nature of writing itself
2. I could write about an idea that fascinates me—like the concept of "untranslatable words" or how maps shape thinking
3. I could write a meditation on something everyday but profound—like waiting, or doorways, or the physics of soap bubbles
4. I could write about the strange beauty of information theory, or why certain numbers appear everywhere
5. I could write about libraries, or marginalia, or the history of footnotes

Let me pick something I can write about with genuine curiosity and texture. I'm drawn to the idea of writing about... let me think. Something like "the joy of obscure knowledge" or "what it's like to think" might be too self-referential. 

What about writing about something concrete and fascinating: the history and philosophy of maps? Or the secret life of everyday objects? Or the concept of "deep time"? Or I could write about something like the strange fact that we don't know how eels reproduce (well, we know more now, but the mystery of eel migration was legendary—no one had ever observed eels mating in the wild for millennia).

Actually, let me write about something with real texture: the idea of "things that hide in plain sight" — or maybe a piece on liminal spaces and why they fascinate us — or the pleasure of reading footnotes and appendices.

Let me consider: what would make for a genuinely good 1000-word piece of freewriting? Something with:
- A clear voice
- Concrete details and specific examples
- Some intellectual substance
- A bit of wandering but not formlessness
- An actual point or at least an evolving meditation

I'll write about... the strange beauty of unfinished things. Or about maps of imaginary places. Or about the archaeology of everyday language—dead metaphors. 

Dead metaphors! That's a rich topic. All the words we use that were once vivid images and are now worn smooth: "broadcast" (sowing seed), "companion" (one you share bread with), "daisy" (day's eye), "goodbye" (God be with ye), "muscle" (little mouse), "salary" (salt money), "tragedy" (goat song). This gives me concrete material to work with, a real theme (how language carries fossilized history, how we walk around speaking poetry without knowing it), and room to roam.

Alternatively, I could write about the concept of "petrichor" and other words for overlooked phenomena... but dead metaphors gives me more range.

Let me draft a piece: "The Fossils in Our Mouths" or "Speaking in Ruins" — a meditation on dead metaphors and the archaeology of everyday speech.

Structure:
1. Opening: the realization that ordinary speech is full of buried images
2. Examples with texture: companion, salary, daisy, muscle, broadcast, tragedy
3. What this means: we're all unwitting poets; language is a palimpsest; metaphor is how thought works, not decoration
4. The process by which metaphors die—repetition wears away the image, like a coin's face rubbed smooth
5. New metaphors being born right now (computer terms: mouse, window, cloud, wallpaper—already dying)
6. What it feels like to notice—the world briefly becomes strange and vivid again
7. Closing thought: maybe meaning itself works this way; maybe all abstraction is built on buried concreteness; we think in metaphors all the way down (Lakoff & Johnson: argument is war, time is money)

That's a solid piece. Let me aim for roughly 1000 words. I should write it well—varied sentences, concrete examples, a voice that's curious and slightly wry.
